claim: Neuronal circuits in the idling brain transition between periods of sustained firing (UP state) and quiescence (DOWN state).
source: In the idling brain, neuronal circuits transition between periods of sustained firing (UP state) and quiescence (DOWN state), a pattern the mechanisms of which remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon in neuroscience.

claim: UP and DOWN durations in spontaneous cortical population activity from anesthetized rats are highly variable.
source: Here we analyzed spontaneous cortical population activity from anesthetized rats and found that UP and DOWN durations were highly variable
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis presented in the manuscript, specifically shown in Figure 2.

claim: Population rates showed no significant decay during UP periods in spontaneous cortical activity from anesthetized rats.
source: Here we analyzed spontaneous cortical population activity from anesthetized rats and found that UP and DOWN durations were highly variable and that population rates showed no significant decay during UP periods.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Adaptation in E cells paradoxically causes a marginal decay of E-rate but a marked decay of I-rate in UP periods.
source: Fluctuations triggered state transitions, while adaptation in E cells paradoxically caused a marginal decay of E-rate but a marked decay of I-rate in UP periods, a prediction that we validated experimentally.
evidence: This prediction from the model was validated with experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: DOWN-to-UP transitions must be caused by synchronous high-amplitude events.
source: A spiking network implementation further predicted that DOWN-to-UP transitions must be caused by synchronous high-amplitude events.
evidence: This is a prediction from the spiking network model implementation described in the manuscript.

claim: Cortical UP and DOWN dynamics take place during slow-wave-sleep (SWS).
source: Cortical UP and DOWN dynamics take place during slow-wave-sleep (SWS) (Steriade et al., 1993a)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Cortical UP and DOWN dynamics can be induced by a number of anesthetics.
source: Cortical UP and DOWN dynamics take place during slow-wave-sleep (SWS) (Steriade et al., 1993a) and can also be induced by a number of anesthetics (Steriade et al., 1993a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Similar synchronous cortical dynamics have been observed in awake rodents during quiescence.
source: More recently however, similar synchronous cortical dynamics have been observed not only in awake rodents during quiescence (Luczak et al., 2007; Petersen et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Similar synchronous cortical dynamics have been observed in animals performing a perceptual task, both rodents and monkeys.
source: More recently however, similar synchronous cortical dynamics have been observed not only in awake rodents during quiescence (Luczak et al., 2007; Petersen et al., 2003), but also in animals performing a perceptual task, both rodents (Sachidhanandam et al., 2013; Vyazovskiy et al., 2011) and monkeys (Engel et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spontaneous activity resembling UP and DOWN states has been found in cortical slices in vitro.
source: Spontaneous activity resembling UP and DOWN states has been found in cortical slices in vitro (Cossart et al., 2003; Fanselow and Connors, 2010; Mann et al., 2009; Sanchez-Vives and McCormick, 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spontaneous activity resembling UP and DOWN states has been found in slabs and in vivo under extensive thalamic lesions.
source: Spontaneous activity resembling UP and DOWN states has been found in cortical slices in vitro (Cossart et al., 2003; Fanselow and Connors, 2010; Mann et al., 2009; Sanchez-Vives and McCormick, 2000), in slabs (Timofeev et al., 2000) and in vivo under extensive thalamic lesions (Steriade et al., 1993b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mechanism underlying UP-DOWN states has an intracortical origin.
source: This suggests that the underlying mechanism has an intracortical origin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that UP-DOWN states occur in cortical slices and under thalamic lesions.

claim: During UP periods a fatigue mechanism of cellular origin decreases network excitability until the cortical network switches into a DOWN state.
source: In such scenario, the standard hypothesis postulates that during UP periods a fatigue mechanism of cellular origin – e.g. spike frequency adaptation currents or synaptic short-term depression – decreases network excitability until the state of tonic firing can no longer be sustained and the cortical network switches into a DOWN state (Contreras et al., 1996; Sanchez-Vives and McCormick, 2000).
evidence: This is described as the standard hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: During DOWN periods, in the absence of firing, the fatigue variables recover until the circuit becomes self-excitable and autonomously transitions into an UP state.
source: During DOWN periods, in the absence of firing, the fatigue variables recover until the circuit becomes self-excitable and autonomously transitions into an UP state (Cunningham et al., 2006; Le Bon-Jego and Yuste, 2007; Poskanzer and Yuste, 2011; Sanchez-Vives and McCormick, 2000; Timofeev et al., 2000).
evidence: This is described as part of the standard hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: The mechanism of activity dependent negative feedback causing oscillatory UP-DOWN dynamics has been implemented by several computational models.
source: This mechanism of activity dependent negative feedback causing oscillatory UP-DOWN dynamics has been implemented by several computational models (Bazhenov et al., 2002; Benita et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2012; Compte et al., 2003b; Ghorbani et al., 2012; Hill and Tononi, 2005; Parga and Abbott, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous computational modeling studies.

claim: The rhythmicity of UP-DOWN dynamics has not been systematically quantified and seems to depend on the details of the preparation.
source: However, although commonly described as a slow oscillation, the rhythmicity of UP-DOWN dynamics has not been systematically quantified and seems to depend on the details of the preparation (Chauvette et al., 2011; Erchova et al., 2002; Lampl et al., 1999; Ruiz-Mejias et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: UP-DOWN transitions in neocortical circuits are coupled with activity in subcortical and limbic areas.
source: Alternatively, there is strong evidence suggesting that UP-DOWN transitions in neocortical circuits are coupled with activity in subcortical and limbic areas.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the following sentences.

claim: Thalamocortical neurons can endogenously oscillate at low frequencies.
source: Thalamocortical neurons for instance can endogenously oscillate at low frequencies (Hughes et al., 2002; McCormick and Pape, 1990)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Thalamocortical neurons cause cortical UP states when stimulated.
source: Thalamocortical neurons for instance can endogenously oscillate at low frequencies (Hughes et al., 2002; McCormick and Pape, 1990), cause cortical UP states when stimulated (Rigas and Castro-Alamancos, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Thalamocortical neurons modulate the UP-DOWN dynamics when suppressed.
source: Thalamocortical neurons for instance can endogenously oscillate at low frequencies (Hughes et al., 2002; McCormick and Pape, 1990), cause cortical UP states when stimulated (Rigas and Castro-Alamancos, 2007) or modulate the UP-DOWN dynamics when suppressed (David et al., 2013; Lemieux et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spontaneous activity of thalamocortical neurons correlates with UP state onset.
source: Thalamocortical neurons for instance can endogenously oscillate at low frequencies (Hughes et al., 2002; McCormick and Pape, 1990), cause cortical UP states when stimulated (Rigas and Castro-Alamancos, 2007) or modulate the UP-DOWN dynamics when suppressed (David et al., 2013; Lemieux et al., 2014) and their spontaneous activity correlates with UP state onset (Contreras and Steriade, 1995; Slézia et al., 2011; Ushimaru et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The timing of hippocampal sharp-wave ripples tends to precede DOWN to UP transitions.
source: Moreover, the timing of hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (Battaglia et al., 2004), or basal ganglia activity (Ushimaru et al., 2012) also tends to precede DOWN to UP transitions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Basal ganglia activity tends to precede DOWN to UP transitions.
source: Moreover, the timing of hippocampal sharp-wave ripples (Battaglia et al., 2004), or basal ganglia activity (Ushimaru et al., 2012) also tends to precede DOWN to UP transitions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Intracortical stimulation can effectively cause UP-DOWN transitions.
source: Finally, intracortical stimulation can effectively cause UP-DOWN transitions (Beltramo et al., 2013; Shu et al., 2003) even when only a few dozen neurons are stimulated (Stroh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Intracortical stimulation can cause UP-DOWN transitions even when only a few dozen neurons are stimulated.
source: Finally, intracortical stimulation can effectively cause UP-DOWN transitions (Beltramo et al., 2013; Shu et al., 2003) even when only a few dozen neurons are stimulated (Stroh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The macroscopic UP-DOWN dynamics are sensitive to temporal fluctuations of both external inputs and local circuit activity.
source: In total, these findings describe a system whose macroscopic UP-DOWN dynamics are sensitive to temporal fluctuations of both external inputs and local circuit activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited evidence about thalamic, hippocampal, and stimulation effects.

claim: A network sensitive to temporal fluctuations would generate unpredictable and irregular UP-DOWN dynamics.
source: Such a network would in principle generate unpredictable and therefore irregular UP-DOWN dynamics, since transitions are no longer dependent exclusively on local cortical internal dynamics.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the sensitivity to fluctuations.

claim: The interplay of fatigue mechanisms and fluctuations causing transitions between two states has been theoretically studied in the developing spinal cord.
source: The interplay of fatigue mechanisms and fluctuations causing transitions between two states has been theoretically studied in the developing spinal cord (Tabak et al., 2011; 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical studies.

claim: The interplay of fatigue mechanisms and fluctuations has been studied in the context of UP-DOWN dynamics mostly in networks composed of excitatory units.
source: The interplay of fatigue mechanisms and fluctuations causing transitions between two states has been theoretically studied in the developing spinal cord (Tabak et al., 2011; 2000), and in the context of UP-DOWN dynamics mostly in networks composed of excitatory units (Holcman and Tsodyks, 2006; Lim and Rinzel, 2010; Mattia and Sanchez-Vives, 2012; Mejias et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: Most models of spontaneous activity are theoretically founded on the balance between excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) populations.
source: Most models of spontaneous activity are however theoretically founded on the balance between excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) populations (Amit and Brunel, 1997; van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1998)
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational modeling work.

claim: A balanced dynamic state can quantitatively mimic population spiking activity during desynchronized states.
source: Most models of spontaneous activity are however theoretically founded on the balance between excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) populations (Amit and Brunel, 1997; van Vreeswijk and Sompolinsky, 1998), a dynamic state that can quantitatively mimic population spiking activity during desynchronized states (Renart et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Analysis of cortical responses in the visual cortex suggest that cortical networks operate in the inhibition-stabilized regime.
source: Analysis of cortical responses in the visual cortex suggest that cortical networks operate in the inhibition-stabilized regime, in which recurrent excitatory feedback alone is strong enough to destabilize the network activity but feedback inhibition maintains stability (Ozeki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental study.

claim: In the inhibition-stabilized regime, recurrent excitatory feedback alone is strong enough to destabilize the network activity but feedback inhibition maintains stability.
source: Analysis of cortical responses in the visual cortex suggest that cortical networks operate in the inhibition-stabilized regime, in which recurrent excitatory feedback alone is strong enough to destabilize the network activity but feedback inhibition maintains stability (Ozeki et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a definition of the inhibition-stabilized regime supported by citation.

claim: The interaction between E and I populations is critical in generating spontaneous activity.
source: In spite of growing evidence showing that the interaction between E and I populations is critical in generating spontaneous activity
evidence: This is stated as growing evidence in the field.

claim: The conditions under which an EI network model can exhibit robust bistability between a low-rate inhibition-stabilized state and a quiescent state are not well understood.
source: In spite of growing evidence showing that the interaction between E and I populations is critical in generating spontaneous activity, the conditions under which an EI network model can exhibit a robust bistability between a low-rate inhibition-stabilized state and a quiescent state are still not well understood (Latham et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge with citation.

claim: Population recordings were performed from anesthetized rats under urethane anesthesia.
source: To develop such a model, we first performed population recordings of ongoing cortical activity during synchronized brain state epochs in rats under urethane anesthesia (Détári and Vanderwolf, 1987; Luczak et al., 2007; Murakami et al., 2005; Whitten et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Analysis of population single-unit spiking dynamics showed irregular UP and DOWN periods.
source: Analysis of population single-unit spiking dynamics, showed irregular UP and DOWN periods and no decay of the average rate during UPs.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data analysis.

claim: The EI network model exhibited a novel type of bistability with a quiescent (DOWN) and a low-rate state (UP).
source: Given these constraints, we built an EI network model that, capitalizing on the firing threshold non-linearity and the asymmetry of the E and I transfer functions, exhibited a novel type of bistability with a quiescent (DOWN) and a low-rate state (UP).
evidence: This describes a key feature of the computational model developed in the study.

claim: External input fluctuations into the network caused the irregular UP-DOWN transitions.
source: External input fluctuations into the network caused the irregular UP-DOWN transitions.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Adaptation in E cells did not cause transitions in the model.
source: Adaptation in E cells in contrast, did not cause transitions
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Adaptation exhibited recovery during DOWN periods in the model.
source: Adaptation in E cells in contrast, did not cause transitions and had a different effect on the E rate in each of the two states: while it exhibited recovery during DOWN periods
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: Adaptation showed almost no decay during UP periods due to the balanced nature of the UP dynamics.
source: Adaptation in E cells in contrast, did not cause transitions and had a different effect on the E rate in each of the two states: while it exhibited recovery during DOWN periods, it showed almost no decay during UP periods due to the balanced nature of the UP dynamics.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: External input fluctuations to neurons in the network cannot respond to simple independent Gaussian statistics.
source: In addition, a spiking network implementation of the model revealed that external input fluctuations to neurons in the network cannot respond to simple independent Gaussian statistics but must include stochastic, synchronous high-amplitude events that can trigger DOWN-to-UP transitions.
evidence: This is a finding from the spiking network model implementation.

claim: External input fluctuations must include stochastic, synchronous high-amplitude events that can trigger DOWN-to-UP transitions.
source: In addition, a spiking network implementation of the model revealed that external input fluctuations to neurons in the network cannot respond to simple independent Gaussian statistics but must include stochastic, synchronous high-amplitude events that can trigger DOWN-to-UP transitions.
evidence: This is a prediction from the spiking network model.

claim: The model provides the first EI network that exhibits stochastic transitions between a silent and a low rate inhibition-stabilized attractor matching the statistics of UP and DOWN periods observed in the cortex.
source: Our model provides the first EI network that exhibits stochastic transitions between a silent and a low rate inhibition-stabilized attractor matching the statistics of UP and DOWN periods and population rate time-courses observed in the cortex.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and contribution of the model.

claim: Spiking activity was recorded from large populations of neurons (mean ±SD = 64±23 cells) in deep layers of somatosensory cortex of urethane-anesthetized rats (n = 7 animals).
source: To investigate the mechanisms underlying the generation of spontaneous cortical activity, we recorded the spiking activity from large populations of neurons (mean ±SD = 64±23 cells) in deep layers of somatosensory cortex of urethane-anesthetized rats (n = 7 animals) (Barthó et al., 2004; Luczak et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods and sample size.

claim: Brain state under urethane can vary spontaneously.
source: Because brain state under urethane can vary spontaneously (Détári and Vanderwolf, 1987; Luczak et al., 2007; Murakami et al., 2005; Whitten et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The most clearly synchronized epochs were characterized by the stable presence of high-amplitude, slow fluctuations in cortical local field potential (LFP) signals.
source: Because brain state under urethane can vary spontaneously (Détári and Vanderwolf, 1987; Luczak et al., 2007; Murakami et al., 2005; Whitten et al., 2009), we selected the most clearly synchronized epochs characterized by the stable presence of high-amplitude, slow fluctuations in cortical local field potential (LFP) signals (Figure 1A; see Materials and methods) (Harris and Thiele, 2011; Steriade et al., 2001).
evidence: This describes the selection criteria for data analysis with supporting citations.

claim: The cortical circuit might transition between two network states in a random manner.
source: Motivated by this, we hypothesized that the cortical circuit might transition between two network states in a random manner (Deco et al., 2009; Mejias et al., 2010; Mochol et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis motivated by the lack of rhythmicity, with supporting citations.

claim: The statistics of U and D period durations showed skewed gamma-like distributions.
source: The statistics of U and D period durations showed skewed gamma-like distributions (Figure 2A and B right; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mean duration of U and D periods across different experiments displayed a wide range of values (mean ±SD:<U>= 0.43 ± 0.19 s, <D> = 0.46 ± 0.1 s, n = 7).
source: The mean duration across different experiments displayed a wide range of values (Figure 2B left; mean ±SD:<U>= 0.43 ± 0.19 s, <D> = 0.46 ± 0.1 s, n = 7)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B with specific statistical values.

claim: The coefficients of variation CV(U) and CV(D) of U and D periods were systematically high (mean ±SD: CV(U) = 0.68 ± 0.09, CV(D) = 0.69 ± 0.1; median CV(U) = 0.64, CV(D) = 0.71).
source: whereas the coefficients of variation CV(U) and CV(D) of U and D periods, defined as the standard deviation divided by the mean of the period durations within experiments, were systematically high (Figure 2B middle, mean ±SD: CV(U) = 0.68 ± 0.09, CV(D) = 0.69 ± 0.1; median CV(U) = 0.64, CV(D) = 0.71).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B with specific statistical values.

claim: The irregularity in the U and D periods did not result from slow drifts in the mean U or D durations caused by variations of brain state.
source: The irregularity in the U and D periods did not result from slow drifts in the mean U or D durations caused by variations of brain state as confirmed by computing the CV2 (Holt et al., 1996), a local measure of irregularity that is less affected by slow variations in the statistics (mean ±SD: CV2(U) = 0.86 ± 0.13, CV2(D) = 0.75 ± 0.17; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by CV2 analysis with specific statistical values and citation.

claim: The high variability of U and D periods is consistent with the non-periodicity of the dynamics revealed in the autocorrelation function.
source: The high variability of U and D periods is consistent with the non-periodicity of the dynamics revealed in the autocorrelation function (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the variability to the autocorrelation results.

claim: D duration (Di) vs the consecutive U duration (Ui) exhibit weak but significant serial correlation.
source: Left: D duration (Di) vs the consecutive U duration (Ui) exhibit weak but significant serial correlation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C with statistical analysis.

claim: Period duration correlation is limited to adjacent periods.
source: whereas it remained close to zero for the rest of lags, showing that period duration correlation is limited to adjacent periods (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: The positive correlation between adjacent periods was not due to slow changes in their duration.
source: The positive correlation between adjacent periods was not due to slow changes in their duration, as we corrected by the correlation obtained from surrogate D-U sequences obtained from shuffling the original sequence within 30 s windows (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by the shuffling control analysis described in methods.

claim: Positive correlations between consecutive periods of activity and silence can be generated when fluctuation driven transitions are combined with an adaptive process.
source: Positive correlations between consecutive periods of activity and silence can be generated when fluctuation driven transitions are combined with an adaptive process such as activity-dependent adaptation currents (Lim and Rinzel, 2010; Tabak et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: A major role of adaptation currents in dictating UP-DOWN dynamics seems at odds with the lack of rhythmicity and the highly variable U and D durations.
source: However, a major role of adaptation currents in dictating UP-DOWN dynamics (Compte et al., 2003b) seems at odds with the lack of rhythmicity and the highly variable U and D durations, indicative of a stochastic mechanism causing the transitions between network states.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed data characteristics.

claim: The mean firing rate in U periods was low (mean ±SD: 3.72 ± 0.9 spikes/s, n = 7).
source: The mean firing rate in U periods was low (mean ±SD: 3.72 ± 0.9 spikes/s, n = 7).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the experimental data.

claim: D periods displayed occasional spiking (mean ±SD rate 0.018 ± 0.007 spikes/s).
source: Moreover, D periods displayed occasional spiking (mean ±SD rate 0.018 ± 0.007 spikes/s; see e.g. Figure 3A–B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A-B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: DOWN periods displaying occasional spiking is in contrast with the idea that DOWN periods do not display spiking activity.
source: Moreover, D periods displayed occasional spiking (mean ±SD rate 0.018 ± 0.007 spikes/s; see e.g. Figure 3A–B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), in contrast with the idea that DOWN periods do not display spiking activity (Chauvette et al., 2010), but see (Compte et al., 2003b).
evidence: This contrasts the finding with previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: There was no significant mean difference between population average rate at U-onset and U-offset windows across experiments (mean ±SD onset minus offset population rate 0.04 ± 0.40 spikes/s, p=1, Wilcoxon signed rank, n = 7 animals).
source: We found no significant mean difference between population average rate at U-onset and U-offset windows across our experiments (mean ±SD onset minus offset population rate 0.04 ± 0.40 spikes/s, p=1, Wilcoxon signed rank, n = 7 animals).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: There was a small but significant mean increase in the population rate between the D-onset and D-offset windows (mean ±SD −0.014 ± 0.013 spikes/s, p=0.047, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
source: The equivalent analysis performed on D periods yielded a small but significant mean increase in the population rate between the D-onset and D-offset windows (mean ±SD −0.014 ± 0.013 spikes/s, p=0.047, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The change between U-onset and U-offset averaged across all neurons (n = 448 cells) was not significantly different from zero (mean ±SD of the onset vs offset difference of normalized rates 0.057 ± 1.163, p=0.12, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
source: We found that the change between U-onset and U-offset averaged across all our neurons (n = 448 cells) was not significantly different from zero (Figure 3E right, mean ±SD of the onset vs offset difference of normalized rates 0.057 ± 1.163, p=0.12, Wilcoxon signed rank test)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The recovery during D periods was significant (mean ±SD −0.015 ± 0.087, p=0.0002, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
source: but that the recovery during D periods was significant (Figure 3E left; mean ±SD −0.015 ± 0.087, p=0.0002, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Some individual neurons showed a significant modulation between U-onset and U-offset, but the decrease found in a fraction of the neurons was compensated with a comparable increase in another fraction of neurons.
source: Some individual neurons however did show a significant modulation between U-onset and U-offset, but the decrease found in a fraction of the neurons was compensated with a comparable increase in another fraction of neurons (Figure 3E right).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: At the population level, spiking activity during U periods displayed a sustained time course with no significant traces of rate adaptation.
source: Thus, at the population level, spiking activity during U periods displayed a sustained time course with no significant traces of rate adaptation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the data analysis.

claim: The EI network model described the dynamics of the mean instantaneous rates rE and rI of each population in the presence of fluctuating external inputs.
source: The excitatory-inhibitory (EI) network model described the dynamics of the mean instantaneous rates rE and rI of each population in the presence of fluctuating external inputs.
evidence: This describes the structure of the computational model.

claim: The E population in the model included an adaptation mechanism, an additive hyperpolarizing current a that grew linearly with the rate rE.
source: In addition, the E population included an adaptation mechanism, an additive hyperpolarizing current a that grew linearly with the rate rE (Figure 4A; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes a feature of the computational model shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Inhibitory neurons show little or no spike-frequency adaptation when depolarized with injected current.
source: We did not consider adaptation in the inhibitory population for simplicity, and because inhibitory neurons show little or no spike-frequency adaptation when depolarized with injected current (McCormick et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The model aimed to search for a regime in which the network exhibited bistability between a quiescent (D) and a low-rate state (U) fixed point in the absence of adaptation and external input fluctuations.
source: Our aim was to search for a regime in which, in the absence of adaptation and external input fluctuations, the network exhibited bistability between a quiescent (D) and a low-rate state (U) fixed point.
evidence: This describes the goal of the modeling work.

claim: Bistability in low-dimensional EI networks has been described since the seminal work of Wilson and Cowan (1972).
source: Although bistability in low-dimensional EI networks has been described since the seminal work of Wilson and Cowan (1972)
evidence: This is supported by citation to foundational work.

claim: Previous models primarily sought to explain bistability between a low-rate and a high-rate state.
source: Although bistability in low-dimensional EI networks has been described since the seminal work of Wilson and Cowan (1972), previous models primarily sought to explain bistability between a low-rate and a high-rate state
evidence: This is a characterization of previous modeling work with citations.

claim: The expansive nonlinearity of the transfer function alone was sufficient to obtain bistability between D and U states.
source: We found that the expansive nonlinearity of the transfer function alone was sufficient to obtain bistability between D and U states.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis.

claim: A threshold-linear function was chosen as the simplest possible transfer function with a threshold.
source: Given this, we chose the simplest possible transfer function with a threshold: a threshold-linear function (Figure 4B, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes a modeling choice shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Only when the I nullcline was shifted to the right and had a larger slope than the E nullcline, the system exhibited two stable attractors.
source: only when the I nullcline was shifted to the right and had a larger slope than the E nullcline, the system exhibited two stable attractors (Equation 20 in Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a finding from the mathematical analysis of the model.

claim: The configuration of the nullclines was readily obtained by setting the threshold and the gain of the I transfer function larger than those of the E transfer function.
source: This configuration of the nullclines was readily obtained by setting the threshold and the gain of the I transfer function larger than those of the E transfer function (Figure 4B)
evidence: This describes how the bistability was achieved in the model, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The difference in gains and thresholds in the E and I populations is a distinctive feature previously reported when intracellularly characterizing the f - I curve of pyramidal and fast spiking interneurons in the absence of background synaptic activity.
source: a distinctive feature previously reported when intracellularly characterizing the f - I curve of pyramidal and fast spiking interneurons in the absence of background synaptic activity (Cruikshank et al., 2007; Schiff and Reyes, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: The difference in gains and thresholds in the E and I populations was not a necessary condition to obtain the bistability.
source: This difference in gains and thresholds in the E and I populations was not a necessary condition to obtain the bistability: alternatively, a proper selection of connectivity parameters with identical E and I transfer functions could satisfy the conditions to obtain similar bistable function (see Materials and methods, Equations [20-22]).
evidence: This is explained in the mathematical analysis in Materials and methods.

claim: The novel bistable regime yielded a quiescent D state, and arbitrarily low firing rates for both E and I populations during U states.
source: This novel bistable regime yielded a quiescent D state, and arbitrarily low firing rates for both E and I populations during U states, depending on the values of the thresholds and the synaptic weights (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In most bistable network models the rate of the sustained activity state is constrained to be above certain lower bound.
source: This is remarkable as in most bistable network models the rate of the sustained activity state is constrained to be above certain lower bound (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous models discussed in the Discussion section.

claim: In the bistable regime, the U state is an inhibition-stabilized state.
source: Moreover, in this bistable regime, the U state is an inhibition-stabilized state, a network dynamical condition in which the excitatory feedback is so strong that would alone be unstable, but is balanced with fast and strong inhibitory feedback to maintain the rates stable (Ozeki et al., 2009; Tsodyks et al., 1997) (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a characterization of the U state in the model with supporting citations.

claim: Transitions between U and D states can occur driven by external input fluctuations.
source: There are two ways in which transitions between U and D states can occur. On the one hand, transitions could be driven by external input fluctuations, which were modeled as a stochastic process with zero mean and short time constant (Figure 4D).
evidence: This describes one mechanism for transitions in the model shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Fluctuating input reflected either afferents coming from other brain areas whose neuronal activity was stochastic and uncorrelated with the cortical circuit internal dynamics or the stochasticity of the spiking happening during U periods.
source: This fluctuating input reflected either afferents coming from other brain areas whose neuronal activity was stochastic and uncorrelated with the cortical circuit internal dynamics or the stochasticity of the spiking happening during U periods which was not captured by the dynamics of the rates (Holcman and Tsodyks, 2006; Lim and Rinzel, 2010).
evidence: This explains the interpretation of the fluctuating input in the model with supporting citations.

claim: In the absence of fluctuations, state transitions could also occur solely driven by adaptation currents.
source: On the other hand, in the absence of fluctuations, state transitions could also occur solely driven by adaptation currents (Figure 4E).
evidence: This describes another mechanism for transitions in the model shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The dynamics of the rates rE(t) and rI(t) relaxing rapidly to their steady-state can be decoupled from the slow changes in a(t) because the adaptation time constant was much longer than the time constants of the E and I rates.
source: Because the adaptation time constant was much longer than the time constants of the E and I rates, the dynamics of the rates rE(t) and rI(t) relaxing rapidly to their steady-state can be decoupled from the slow changes in a(t) (Latham et al., 2000; Rinzel and Lee, 1987).
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the model with supporting citations.

claim: During U periods the build-up in adaptation produced a downward displacement of the E-nullcline.
source: In particular, during U periods the build-up in adaptation produced a downward displacement of the E-nullcline (Figure 4E).
evidence: This describes the effect of adaptation in the model shown in Figure 4E.

claim: If adaptation strength β was sufficiently large the displacement increased until the U state was no longer a fixed point and the network transitioned to the only stable fixed point D.
source: If adaptation strength β was sufficiently large the displacement increased until the U state was no longer a fixed point and the network transitioned to the only stable fixed point D.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of adaptation-driven transitions in the model.

claim: Recovery of adaptation during D periods shifted the E-nullcline upwards until the D state disappeared and there was a transition to the U state.
source: Recovery of adaptation during D periods shifted the E-nullcline upwards until the D state disappeared and there was a transition to the U state (Figure 4E).
evidence: This describes the mechanism of adaptation recovery in the model shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In the limit cycle regime the network exhibited an oscillatory behavior with a frequency close to the inverse of the adaptation recovery time constant.
source: In this limit cycle regime the network exhibited an oscillatory behavior with a frequency close to the inverse of the adaptation recovery time constant.
evidence: This describes the behavior in the limit cycle regime of the model.

claim: Metastable refers to a state that was stable to the dynamics of both the rates and the adaptation but could transition away due to input fluctuations.
source: When the two types of transitions are combined, two types of stability in U and D states can be distinguished: (1) metastable, referred to a state that was stable to the dynamics of both the rates and the adaptation but could transition away due to input fluctuations
evidence: This is a definition of metastability in the context of the model.

claim: Quasi-stable refers to a state that was stable for the fast rate dynamics but unstable for the slow adaptation dynamics, plus it was also susceptible to fluctuation-driven transitions.
source: (2) quasi-stable, referred to a state that was stable for the fast rate dynamics but unstable for the slow adaptation dynamics, plus it was also susceptible to fluctuation-driven transitions.
evidence: This is a definition of quasi-stability in the context of the model.

claim: Only metastable states tend to give exponentially distributed durations with CV ~1.
source: Since only metastable states tend to give exponentially distributed durations with CV ~1, the large variability found in both U and D durations (Figure 2B) constrained the model to the subregion where both states were metastable and UD and DU transitions were driven by fluctuations (red area in Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a theoretical property used to constrain the model parameters.

claim: The large variability found in both U and D durations constrained the model to the subregion where both states were metastable and UD and DU transitions were driven by fluctuations.
source: Since only metastable states tend to give exponentially distributed durations with CV ~1, the large variability found in both U and D durations (Figure 2B) constrained the model to the subregion where both states were metastable and UD and DU transitions were driven by fluctuations (red area in Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes how the experimental data constrained the model parameters, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The existence of serial correlations between consecutive U and D in the data discarded an adaptation-free regime (β = 0).
source: The existence of serial correlations between consecutive U and D in the data (Figure 2C–D) discarded an adaptation-free regime (β = 0), in which transitions were solely driven by fluctuations and the duration of each period was independent of previous durations (Figure 5B right).
evidence: This describes how the experimental data constrained the model parameters.

claim: In an adaptation-free regime (β = 0), transitions were solely driven by fluctuations and the duration of each period was independent of previous durations.
source: The existence of serial correlations between consecutive U and D in the data (Figure 2C–D) discarded an adaptation-free regime (β = 0), in which transitions were solely driven by fluctuations and the duration of each period was independent of previous durations (Figure 5B right).
evidence: This describes the properties of the adaptation-free regime in the model.

claim: The model with β >0 in the region where both states were metastable produced alternation dynamics with broad U and D duration distributions and relatively high CVs.
source: Thus, we explored a regime with β >0 but still in the region where both states were metastable (Figure 5B, green square) and the input fluctuations produced alternation dynamics (Figure 5C top) with broad U and D duration distributions and relatively high CVs (Figure 5D top).
evidence: This describes the model behavior in a specific parameter regime shown in Figures 5B-D.

claim: The magnitude of the fluctuations was adjusted to obtain frequent transitions and serial correlations quantitatively comparable with the data.
source: The magnitude of the fluctuations was adjusted to obtain frequent transitions in this region and serial correlations quantitatively comparable with the data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the parameter tuning in the model shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rates showed an autocorrelation function qualitatively similar to the data, with negative side-lobes but no clear traces of rhythmicity.
source: Moreover, the rates showed an autocorrelation function qualitatively similar to the data, with negative side-lobes but no clear traces of rhythmicity (Figure 5E).
evidence: This compares the model output to the experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Adaptation introduced correlations across consecutive periods because at the transition times the system kept a memory of the previous period in the adaptation value a(t).
source: Adaptation introduced correlations across consecutive periods (Figure 5D bottom) because at the transition times the system kept a memory of the previous period in the adaptation value a(t).
evidence: This explains the mechanism for serial correlations in the model shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Adaptation had to be fast, to vary within one period, but not too fast to prevent reaching the equilibrium.
source: a condition that required adaptation to be fast, to vary within one period, but not too fast to prevent reaching the equilibrium (Figure 5C bottom trace).
evidence: This describes the constraint on adaptation timescale shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the regime explored, the dynamics of adaptation a(t) alone did not cause transitions but did strongly modulate the probability that an external fluctuation would cause a transition.
source: In this regime, the dynamics of adaptation a(t) alone did not cause transitions but did strongly modulate the probability that an external fluctuation would cause a transition (Moreno-Bote et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the role of adaptation in the model with supporting citation.

claim: The observed U-D dynamics occurred in a regime with strong random fluctuations, that these fluctuations were necessary to cause the transitions, and that adaptation modulated the timing of the transitions and consequently introduced correlations between the duration of consecutive periods.
source: Altogether, this analysis suggests that the observed U-D dynamics occurred in a regime with strong random fluctuations, that these fluctuations were necessary to cause the transitions, and that adaptation modulated the timing of the transitions and consequently introduced correlations between the duration of consecutive periods.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the model analysis.

claim: The average rE(t) at the beginning and at the end of U periods did not show much difference whereas the average rI(t) showed a larger decrease over the U period.
source: Interestingly, the average rE(t) at the beginning and at the end of U periods did not show much difference whereas the average rI(t) showed a larger decrease over the U period (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the model shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Although only the E and not the I population included intrinsic adaptation mechanisms, it was rI(t) the one that exhibited the most pronounced decay during U periods.
source: Thus, although only the E and not the I population included intrinsic adaptation mechanisms, it was rI(t) the one that exhibited the most pronounced decay during U periods.
evidence: This is a counterintuitive finding from the model.

claim: The difference in thresholds (θI > θE) and the fact that the I-nullcline has a higher slope than the E-nullcline caused the downward displacement of the E-nullcline during U periods to produce a greater decrease in rI(t) than in rE(t).
source: This was a direct consequence of the specific conditions that gave rise to bistability in our model: the difference in thresholds, that is, θI > θE, and the fact that the I-nullcline has a higher slope than the E-nullcline (Equation 21 in Materials and methods). These features imposed that as adaptation built up during U periods, the downward displacement of the E-nullcline caused a greater decrease in rI(t) than in rE(t) (compare 'decay' colored bands in Figure 6B).
evidence: This explains the mechanism for the differential decay shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The drop in rE(t) could be made arbitrarily small by increasing the slope of the I-nullcline.
source: With this arrangement the drop in rE(t) could be made arbitrarily small by increasing the slope of the I-nullcline (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a property of the model shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The feature of the model predicting differential decay of E and I rates is not dependent on its specific regime of operation, as it would similarly apply in an adaptation-driven regime.
source: Note that this feature of the model is not dependent on its specific regime of operation, as it would similarly apply in an adaptation-driven regime (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a generalization of the model property with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: During D periods the average rE(t) showed a substantial increase due to the recovery of adaptation, whereas the rI(t) did not.
source: During D periods the average rE(t) did show a substantial increase due to the recovery of adaptation, whereas the rI(t) did not.
evidence: This is a finding from the model.

claim: In the D state, the quiescent network behaved as isolated neurons reflecting the dynamics of intrinsic adaptation which was only present on E cells.
source: This was because in the D state, the quiescent network behaved as isolated neurons reflecting the dynamics of intrinsic adaptation which was only present on E cells.
evidence: This explains the mechanism for the behavior during D periods.

claim: If the majority of the neurons recorded experimentally were excitatory, the model could explain why adaptation currents did not cause a significant decrease in the average rate during U periods.
source: In sum, if the majority of the neurons that we recorded experimentally were excitatory, the model could explain why adaptation currents did not cause a significant decrease in the average rate during U periods (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This connects the model prediction to the experimental observation in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The model predicts that the rate of inhibitory neurons should exhibit a noticeable decrease during U periods.
source: The model in addition predicts that the rate of inhibitory neurons should exhibit a noticeable decrease during U periods.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Isolated units from n = 5 experiments were classified into putative interneurons (I) and putative excitatory neurons (E) based on spike waveforms.
source: Motivated by this prediction, we investigated the dynamics of the rates of excitatory and inhibitory neurons during U and D periods in the experimental data. Based on spike waveforms, isolated units from n = 5 experiments were classified into putative interneurons (I) and putative excitatory neurons (E), following previously described procedures (Barthó et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes the experimental method for cell classification with citation.

claim: I cells displayed a significant rate decay during U periods that was not observed in E cells (mixed-effects ANOVA with factors neuron type (E/I), onset/offset and neuron identity and experiment as random factors: interaction neuron type x onset/offset F(1,349)=6.3, p=0.013).
source: As predicted by the model (Figure 6A-B), I cells displayed a significant rate decay during U periods that was not observed in E cells (Figure 6D; mixed-effects ANOVA with factors neuron type (E/I), onset/offset and neuron identity and experiment as random factors: interaction neuron type x onset/offset F(1,349)=6.3, p=0.013).
evidence: This validates the model prediction with experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: During D periods, E cells showed a significant increase in rate (Wilcoxon signed rank test p=0.0092), whereas no rate change was found in I cells.
source: During D periods, E cells also showed a significant increase in rate (Wilcoxon signed rank test p=0.0092), just like that observed in the whole cell population, whereas no rate change was found in I cells (not shown).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The validation of the prediction on the counter-intuitive emergent dynamics of E and I rates during U periods strongly suggests that the mechanism dissected by the model underlies the putative bistability observed in cortical circuit dynamics.
source: The validation of the prediction on the counter-intuitive emergent dynamics of E and I rates during U periods strongly suggests that the mechanism dissected by the model underlies the putative bistability observed in cortical circuit dynamics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation of the model prediction.

claim: A spiking network composed of NE = 4000 excitatory and NI = 1000 inhibitory leaky integrate-and-fire spiking units was built.
source: To assess whether the mechanism for state transitions proposed by the rate model could generate UP-DOWN dynamics in a more biophysically realistic circuit we built a network composed of NE = 4000 excitatory and NI = 1000 inhibitory leaky integrate-and-fire spiking units (Ricciardi, 1977) (all-to-all connectivity).
evidence: This describes the spiking network model implementation.

claim: Current-based synapses were used in the spiking network and a spike-based after-hyperpolarization (AHP) current was introduced in E cells.
source: We used current-based synapses (Brunel and Sergi, 1998) and introduced a spike-based after-hyperpolarization (AHP) current in E cells (Wang, 1998; La Camera et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes features of the spiking network model with citations.

claim: Using standard mean-field methods, the same network bistability described in the rate model was revealed in the spiking network.
source: The EI asymmetry in spike threshold and f - I gain described in the rate model was implemented and, using standard mean-field methods (Amit and Tsodyks, 1991), we revealed the same network bistability described above (compare Figures 7A and 4C): a saddle node bifurcation gave rise to a quiescent branch (DOWN) co-existing with a low-rate branch (UP; Figure 7B).
evidence: This shows that the spiking network exhibits the same bistability as the rate model, shown in Figures 7A-B.

claim: While the network was in the UP state the AHP current increased moving the system along the upper branch towards the saddle-node and just causing a small decrease in rE.
source: Numerical simulations showed that while the network was in the UP state the AHP current increased moving the system along the upper branch towards the saddle-node and just causing a small decrease in rE.
evidence: This is a finding from the spiking network simulations.

claim: A small AHP amplitude was chosen so that the network operated in the bistable regime and the adaptation buildup alone did not trigger an UP to DOWN transition.
source: However, because we chose a small AHP amplitude so that the network operated in the bistable regime (see fixed points in Figure 7B), the adaptation buildup alone did not trigger an UP to DOWN transition.
evidence: This describes a parameter choice in the spiking network model shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The current fluctuations produced by the irregular activity during UP periods triggered UP to DOWN transitions.
source: It was the current fluctuations produced by the irregular activity during UP periods that triggered UP to DOWN transitions.
evidence: This describes the mechanism for UP to DOWN transitions in the spiking network.

claim: Once the network was in the DOWN state the external independent Gaussian inputs only caused subthreshold membrane fluctuations in E cells that sat far away from the spiking threshold.
source: However, once the network was in the DOWN state the external independent Gaussian inputs only caused subthreshold membrane fluctuations in E cells that sat far away from the spiking threshold (voltage std. dev. 2.5 mV with distance from resting voltage to threshold of 12.4 mV).
evidence: This is a finding from the spiking network simulations.

claim: In the DOWN state with only Gaussian inputs, there was no spiking activity and the network could not transition to the UP state.
source: In these conditions, there was no spiking activity during DOWN periods and the network could not transition to the UP state (not shown).
evidence: This is a finding from the spiking network simulations.

claim: Depolarizing neurons so that their resting potential during the D state was closer to threshold was sufficient to generate UP-DOWN alternations but prevented the membrane potential from showing bi-modality.
source: To make these subthreshold fluctuations effective in driving transitions, we first depolarized neurons so that their resting potential during the D state was closer to threshold and the recovery from adaptation alone was almost sufficient to cause the transitions (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–E). This ad hoc depolarization was sufficient to generate UP-DOWN alternations but prevented the membrane potential from showing bi-modality (Figure 7—figure supplement 2F), the intracellular signature of UP and DOWN states.
evidence: This describes an alternative approach and its limitation shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The alternations with ad hoc depolarization had a very small serial correlation between consecutive D and U periods because adaptation at the time of the DOWN-to-UP transition was narrowly distributed.
source: Moreover, the alternations had a very small serial correlation between consecutive D and U periods, Corr(D,U), (Figure 7—figure supplement 2I) because adaptation at the time of the DOWN-to-UP transition was narrowly distributed, did not retain information about the length of the DOWN period, and could thus not constrain the duration of the following U period (Lim and Rinzel, 2010).
evidence: This explains why the alternative approach failed to reproduce serial correlations, shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2I.

claim: The most parsimonious way to cause a DOWN to UP transition without disrupting the bi-modality of the membrane potential was to introduce stochastic brief external excitatory synchronous inputs.
source: We thus reasoned that the most parsimonious way to cause a DOWN to UP transition without disrupting the bi-modality of the membrane potential was to maintain resting neurons hyperpolarized and to introduce stochastic brief external excitatory synchronous inputs that caused large amplitude depolarizing voltage bumps in a targeted subpopulation of E and I neurons (DeWeese and Zador, 2006).
evidence: This describes the solution implemented in the spiking network model with citation.

claim: The statistics of occurrence times of the synchronous input bumps were Poisson.
source: The statistics of occurrence times of these bumps were Poisson (Tan et al., 2013)
evidence: This describes a feature of the synchronous inputs with citation.

claim: The frequency (~2–3 Hz) and amplitude (~10–15 mV) of the synchronous bumps were set so that they could cause DOWN to UP transitions with non-rhythmic structure and yield U and D interval distributions similar to the data.
source: and their frequency (~2–3 Hz) and amplitude (~10–15 mV) were set so that (i) they could cause DOWN to UP transitions (Figure 7C–E) with non-rhythmic structure (Figure 7G) and yield U and D interval distributions similar to the data (Figure 7H)
evidence: This describes the parameter choices for the synchronous inputs shown in Figures 7C-E, G, H.

claim: Some kicks during DOWN periods failed to cause a transition, giving rise to sporadic sparse firing during DOWN periods.
source: This meant that some kicks during DOWN periods failed to cause a transition, giving rise to sporadic sparse firing during DOWN periods also seen as large bumps in the membrane potential of the targeted cells (see asterisks in Figure 7C; see Discussion).
evidence: This is a finding from the spiking network simulations shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Because of the dependence of the transition probability on the recovery of the AHP current, the transition dynamics displayed serial correlations Corr(D, U).
source: Because of this dependence of the transition probability on the recovery of the AHP current, the transition dynamics displayed serial correlations Corr(D, U) (Figure 7I), as observed in the data (Figure 2C-D).
evidence: This connects the spiking network results in Figure 7I to the experimental data in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Once in the UP state, the external kicks caused an excess of excitatory and especially inhibitory activity that destabilized the UP state and generated a transition to the DOWN state.
source: Once in the UP state, the external kicks caused an excess of excitatory and especially inhibitory activity that destabilized the UP state and generated a transition to the DOWN state.
evidence: This describes the mechanism for UP to DOWN transitions in the spiking network.

claim: Because the effectiveness of the kicks causing UP to DOWN transitions also depended on the average AHP current, there were significant serial correlations Corr(U,D) quantitatively comparable to the data.
source: Because the effectiveness of the kicks causing these transitions also depended on the average AHP current (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F), there were significant serial correlations Corr(U,D) quantitatively comparable to the data (Figure 7I).
evidence: This connects the spiking network results in Figure 7I to the experimental data.

claim: As explained by the rate model, the averaged population rate rE(t) showed very weak decrease along the UP period whereas rI(t) decayed much more strongly, until the overshoot caused by kicks at the UP offset.
source: As explained by the rate model, the averaged population rate rE(t) showed very weak decrease along the UP period whereas rI(t) decayed much more strongly, until the overshoot caused by kicks at the UP offset (Figure 7J).
evidence: This shows that the spiking network reproduces the rate model prediction shown in Figure 7J.

claim: Neurons in the spiking network displayed a bi-modal distribution of the membrane potential.
source: Neurons displayed a bi-modal distribution of the membrane potential (Figure 7F; Figure 7—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: During UP periods neurons in the spiking network fired low rate irregular spike trains (CV of the Inter-spike-interval was 0.74 for E cells and 0.94 for I cells).
source: and during UP periods they fired low rate irregular spike trains (CV of the Inter-spike-interval was 0.74 for E cells and 0.94 for I cells).
evidence: This is a finding from the spiking network simulations.

claim: A spiking network model was able to reproduce the results described in the rate model given there exists a mechanism to generate stochastic, synchronous large-amplitude bumps.
source: In sum, a spiking network model was able to reproduce the results described in the rate model given there exists a mechanism to generate stochastic, synchronous large-amplitude bumps.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the spiking network analysis.
